Data Science Tools (WS 2025/26)

Chapter 7 Data sets

7.1 Overview of four example data sets

In this course Data Science Tools we will only work with very few exemplary data sets:

  1. mtcars: This is a very small dataset, so you can manually check how tidyverse functions work. A description can be obtained from the help function, which can be called using help("mtcars").

  2. german: This data set, dating from the 1950s and publicly available in different variants, comprises the data of 1000 borrowers and is used in this course to illustrate an elementary classification procedure (Naive Bayes) and to illustrate evaluation methods. Note that several variants of this dataset are inconsistent.

  3. nycflights13: This R package contains five separate tables that can be used to illustrate SQL-like tidyverse functions very well. A first overview can be found in the help via help(package = "nycflights13"). Further additions can be found below. Numerous examples of this data set are covered in,20 the standard textbook on the Tidyverse.

  4. A dataset on public households extracted from the GENESIS database system of the Federal Statistical Office of Germany, which illustrates some principles of data preparation and data cleaning. Details are described in chapter 32.

TBD: Example 4 might be complemented or substituted by a data sets provide by EUROSTAT.

Numerous other examples can be found in Baumer et al.21 and in Hadley Wickham and Garret Grolemund22 and Hadley Wickham et al.23 Furthermore, numerous R libraries contain datasets, including the R package datasets (The R Datasets Package) of the basic installation. There is also a huge amount of publicly available and more or less well documented datasets on the Internet, e.g. at Kaggle.

In the following, the second data set german is characterized and explained as an example. Subsequently, some special features of nycflights13 are briefly outlined.

7.2 Data set german (or German Credit)

The dataset German Credit by Prof. Hans Hofmann (University of Hamburg) was deposited in 1994 on the UCI Machine Learning Repository as a CSV file together with documentation. The original dataset uses non-speaking and cryptic variable names (e.g. A3 for credit history) and variable values (e.g. digit 3 for delay in paying off in the past for variable A3) and therefore requires intensive processing.

The date of entry for the data record is unknown, but based on the variable values, it can be assumed that it was in the 1970s.

The Hofmann dataset has been made available by numerous authors in the past in several versions, some with considerably different variable names and variable characteristics, so that the use of an already prepared version is recommended for teaching purposes24. Examples are:

  1. Under Freakonomics you will find the data as a CSV file, which has already been used in this form by several authors (including Charpentier). This version can be read25 and saved26 directly from the URL using the following commands:
> url <- "http://freakonometrics.free.fr/german_credit.csv"
> credit <- read.csv(url, header = TRUE, sep = ",")
> #write.csv(credit, file = "./data/german_credit/freakonometrics/credit.csv")
> #credit <- read.csv(file = "./data/german_credit/freakonometrics/credit.csv")
> dplyr::glimpse(credit)

  1. Under Kaggle you will find several variants of this data set with different descriptions. The associated data description contains a spreadsheet presentation of the data with the most important key figures and graphs. Note that the data on Kaggle includes the variable foreign_worker, where the majority is coded as yes. This is unreasonable, as can be seen from the analysis under point 3.

    Downloading the data from Kaggle data is tedious for two reasons:

    1. Registration with Kaggle is required.
    2. As far as I know (October 27, 2025), there is no official Kaggle API available under CRAN27.

  2. In the library rchallenge the data set is also available as dataframe german in the R package rchallenge. This prepared data set has two essential and decisive advantages:

    1. Nominal scaled variables are available in the data set as unordered factor variables (factor). This facilitates the initial preparation28.

    2. The dataset rchallenge::german contains important corrections by Grömping (2019), who proved that several English-language variants of the original dataset from the 1950s were incorrectly coded due to misinterpretations of the German-language variable names and variable characteristics. These errors were eliminated in the dataframe german in the R package rchallenge. However, there are numerous analyses in circulation based on other data formats that were created on the basis of incorrect variants. These analyses are therefore also incorrect.

Only the data set german from the R package rchallenge is required, but not the other functions and variables. The assignment german <- rchallenge::german avoids having to load the rchallenge package. Loading the rchallenge package with library(rchallenge), on the other hand, would result in all symbols from rchallenge being visible, including those that are not required.

The dataframe german has 1000 observations and 21 variables.

Some variables (savings, employment_duration, status) are strictly speaking ordinal variables that can be converted into ordinal-scaled variables using ordered or as.ordered. As we do not use any special methods for ordinal-scaled variables in this course, this transformation is not used here.

The variable values can also be extracted from the documentation using the string functions available in the R base system and in the Tidyverse-library stringr. Many of these string functions are based on regular expressions.

7.4 Analysis with the R package mosaic

Alternatively, you can use the tally function for discrete variables and the favstats function from the R package mosaic29 for continuous variables; tally also allows several options, some of which are illustrated with the following calls30. The main textbook for this course (Baumer et al.31) mainly uses functions from mosaic for description. Therefore, these functions are also used occasionally in the following chapters.

The R package janitor32, which is much more closely linked to the Tidyverse libraries, contains the function tabyl (callable e.g. with janitor::tabyl), which can be used to prepare up to three-dimensional tables. Supplementary functions such as adorn_totals and adorn_percentages enable the flexible extension of tables with marginal totals, percentage values and other variables.

The direct use of the mosaic functions with the tidyverse is more complex, as the first argument of most mosaic functions usually does not match the data set.

A note: To use a function with the name <fkt> from an installed R library (R package) <rpk>, you can load the library using require(<rpk>) or library(<rpk>) and then call it directly using the function call <fkt>(<args>) with arguments <args>: Alternatively, you can bypass loading the library by using :: and call the function directly using rpk::fkt(<args>).

> mosaic::tally(~savings, data = german)

The first table generates the joint distribution. The second table, on the other hand, shows the conditional percentage distribution of credit risks in good and bad for a given credit history. And the third table shows the second table in transposed form.

These examples also clearly show that it makes sense to use short character strings for categorical characteristic values. Finding these without simultaneously omitting essential information can be very difficult, especially for data sets with numerous variables (e.g. for the Income and Consumer Survey Einkommens- und Verbraucherstichprobe (EVS) (Survey on income, consumption and living conditions).

7.5 Analysis with the R package summarytools

An alternative to the functions used above are the functions available in the summarytools package. These are demonstrated here as examples for some variables. However, you can only obtain readable output with the functions of this library if you format the results with knitr and RMarkdown using the knitr option results = 'asis' and if you explicitly include the library with library(summarytools). Calling summarytools::freq(), on the other hand, often leads to incorrect output. Under Github you will always find the current R package summarytools, which is still under development. Regardless of the installation source, the summarytools package is loaded with library.

> library(summarytools)

The following examples show the variety of descriptive statistics in R. Depending on the problem and the formatting quality requirements, you will decide on an approach or a package.

7.5.1 Descriptive statistics for metric variables

7.5.1.1 Descriptive statistics for amount

The function descr from the package summarytools generates a series of descriptive statistics for metric variables; when applied to non-metric variables (class(<var>) !="numeric") such as savings, however, you will receive an error message.

> descr(german$amount, style = "simple")
Descriptive Statistics  
german$amount  
N: 1000  

                      amount
----------------- ----------
             Mean    3271.25
          Std.Dev    2822.75
              Min     250.00
               Q1    1365.00
           Median    2319.50
               Q3    3972.50
              Max   18424.00
              MAD    1627.15
              IQR    2606.75
               CV       0.86
         Skewness       1.94
      SE.Skewness       0.08
         Kurtosis       4.25
          N.Valid    1000.00
                N    1000.00
        Pct.Valid     100.00

Incidentally, warnings occurred occasionally in earlier versions (e.g. the warning that occurred in 2020: funs() is deprecated as of dplyr 0.8.0.).

Warnings indicating that deprecated functions are being used usually occur when developers do not update their libraries immediately after version changes in R or the Tidyverse. Such warnings can often be ignored temporarily, as outdated functions are often still available in the libraries at the same time as the newer versions33. Only after more extensive version changes (e.g. change of the main version) are the outdated functions removed from a library. However, the developers of the summarytools library adapted the corresponding functions relatively quickly34.

7.6 Summary analysis (summary statistics)

It is also possible to generate a summarized description of all variables of a data.frame. Within RStudio, you can use the dfSummary function to create simple and clear, albeit low-detail displays. Notes on the output:

  1. if view(dfSummary(german)) is executed within RMarkdown, a Data Frame Summary is written to a temporary html file.
  2. if view(dfSummary(german)) is executed within RStudio (via source or console), the corresponding output appears in the RStudio viewer window.
  3. if dfSummary(german) is executed directly in the console, an object with the class memberships summarytools and data.frame is generated, which contains a rough representation with alphanumeric graphics, among other things, in the print output.

The function dfSummary returns a text representation of the summary in all cases, while view returns the temporary HTML file including path as invisible.

Within RMarkdown you can generate a similar, but usually better representation with the following command:

> dfSummary(german, 
+           plain.ascii = FALSE, 
+             style = "grid", 
+             headings = FALSE, 
+             tmp.img.dir = "./tmp",
+             silent = TRUE)

Generating visually appealing tables is generally an art, so you can find numerous tips on the Internet such as How to Make Beautiful Tables in R and Top 7 Packages for Making Beautiful Tables in R as well as several R packages such as the package r2spss on CRAN. These R packages are particularly useful when you need to analyze extensive survey data.

Incidentally, there is a whole range of other packages in R that can be used to calculate summarized statistics. Worth mentioning here is also the package skimr, with which you can save summary statistics in the tibble’s shown in the third chapter and thus feed them into a further evaluation. This package can also be used to generate tables that can be used to create dynamic reports using the functions in RMarkdown and knitr.

Another package is dataMaid. Unfortunately the last revisions of the R package dataMaid are no longer as stable as the versions from previous years. This is why I am increasingly using the R package summarytools, which was described in the previous section.

7.7 Exemplary graphs with `ggplot2

As a preview of the highly practical and, above all, very powerful R library ggplot2, several variables (status, credit_history and amount) are presented graphically as examples. However, the logic behind the functions will be described in the next chapter.

> german |>
+   ggplot(aes(x = savings)) +
+   geom_bar() +
+   theme(axis.text.x = element_text(
+     size = 10, 
+     angle = 90, 
+     vjust = 1, 
+     hjust = 0))

> german |>
+   ggplot(aes(x = amount)) +
+   geom_histogram()
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value
`binwidth`.

> german |>
+   ggplot(aes(x = amount)) +
+   geom_density()

> german |>
+   ggplot(aes(x = amount)) +
+   geom_histogram() +
+   facet_wrap(~credit_risk)
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value
`binwidth`.

> german |>
+   ggplot(aes(x = amount, color = credit_risk)) +
+   geom_freqpoly()
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value
`binwidth`.

> german |>
+   ggplot(aes(x = amount)) +
+   geom_freqpoly(aes(y = after_stat(count)))
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value
`binwidth`.

> german |>
+   ggplot(aes(x = amount, color = credit_risk)) +
+   geom_freqpoly(aes(y = after_stat(count/sum(count))))
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value
`binwidth`.

> german |>
+   ggplot(aes(x = amount, color = credit_risk)) +
+  geom_freqpoly(aes(y = after_stat(density)))   
`stat_bin()` using `bins = 30`. Pick better value
`binwidth`.

The geom_*’s implicitly calculate some statistical quantities from the data, such as frequency or count tables. These are extracted in the current ggplot-geom's with the relatively new auxiliary function after_stat. Until some time ago, however, these statistical variables had to be extracted using poorly documented internal variable names limited by two dots (..) on the left and right side of the symbol name. Examples are

> german |> 
+   ggplot(aes(x = amount)) +
+   geom_freqpoly(aes(y = ..count.. / sum(..count..)))

and

> german |> 
+   ggplot(aes(x = amount, color = credit_risk)) +
+   geom_freqpoly(aes(y = ..density..))   
> # ^alternatively: ..count.. (default), ..ncount.., ..ndensity..

In the meantime, this procedure, which is still frequently used, has been marked as obsolete (deprecated). Accordingly, the last two plot commands generate warning messages such as the following in some old package versions:

# Warning: The dot-dot notation (`..count..`) was deprecated in ggplot2 3.4.0.
# ? Please use `after_stat(count)` instead.

These warnings have now been disabled again.

7.8 Data set nycflights13

Install the library nycflights13 with the data, if not yet available.

> install.packages("nycflights13", dependencies = TRUE)

Loading the library

> library(nycflights13)

The R package nycflights13 used in numerous works contains essential information about American domestic flights that took off from the three commercial airports in New York in 2013. Specifically, these are the following airports:

  • JFK = John F. Kennedy Airport
  • LGA = La Guardia Airport
  • EWR = Newark Airport

The geographical positions can also be displayed on an OpenStreetMap map using a few R commands, whereby the coordinates longitude (lon) and latitude (lat) of the three airports were determined manually using the Coordinates converter for WGS84, UTM, CH1903, UTMREF(MGRS), Gauß-Krüger, NAC, W3W.

> library(OpenStreetMap)
> library(ggimage)
> #library(ggrepel)
> # Coordinates according to https://coordinates-converter.com/en/
> airports_coord <- tribble(
+   ~airport, ~lat, ~lon,
+   "JFK", 40.642948, -73.779373, # JFK = John F. Kennedy Airport
+   "LGA", 40.776927, -73.873966, # LGA = La Guardia Airport, New York
+   "EWR", 40.689064, -74.177255) # EWR = Newark Airport  
> airports_coord
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  airport   lat   lon
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 JFK      40.6 -73.8
2 LGA      40.8 -73.9
3 EWR      40.7 -74.2
> lat <- airports_coord |> 
+   pull(lat)
> lon <- airports_coord |> 
+   pull(lon)
> distance_degree <- 0.1
> # Read OSM map around three New York airports and save it: outcommented
> # airports_new_york <- openmap(
> #   c(min(lat) - distance_degree, min(lon) - distance_degree),
> #   c(max(lat) + distance_degree, max(lon) + distance_degree),
> #   type = "osm")
> # save(airports_new_york, file = "./data/OSM2025/airports_new_york.RData") # Backup copy
> load(file = "./data/OSM2025/airports_new_york.RData")  # load saved file
> # Generate quasi Mercator projection 
> airports_new_york_mercator <- airports_new_york |>  
+ openproj()
> # Plot map with airports
> airports_new_york_mercator |> 
+   autoplot() +
+   geom_image(data = airports_coord,
+              aes(x = lon, y = lat), 
+              image = "./images/Airport_symbol.svg.png",
+              size = 0.07) + 
+   geom_text(data = airports_coord,
+             aes(x = lon - 0.02 , y = lat - 0.02, label = airport),
+             color = "red",
+             fontface = "bold", 
+             size = 4) +
+   labs(title = "Airports New York",
+        subtitle = "Special Mercator projection",
+        x = "Longitude (in °)",
+        y = "Latitude (in °)",
+        caption = "\u00A9 Ulrich Küsters, October 27, 2025")

In detail, the library contains five non-redundant data sets that can be used as so-called tibble-data-frame’s with class tbl_df and thus also via class inheritance as tibbles and as dataframes; see next teaching unit.

  • flights contains all departures in 2013 from JFK, LGA and EWR and includes 336776 cases and 19 variables.
  • airports contains all associated destination airports and includes 1458 destination airports and 8 variables.
  • airlines contains all associated airlines and includes 16 lines and 2 variables.
  • planes contains all associated airplanes (with identifier) and includes 3322 machines and 9 variables.
  • weather contains the weather measurement data for all three airports and includes 26115 METAR reports with 15 variables. METARs are METeorological Aerodrome Reports, see the Wikipedia entry METAR.

The variable descriptions can be found by calling up the documentation, e.g. by entering help(package = "nycflights13") in the console.

The five data records are linked to each other via so-called keys. The data records can be linked together using so-called join operations. Join operations can be realized either with the help of SQL (Structured Query Language) or with the help of the functions implemented in the R library dplyr (as part of tidyverse). The latter are dealt with in detail in the unit DSW-3.

The five tables from nycflights13 are used in the Data Science courses mainly for the following purposes:

  • Demonstration of graphs in ggplot2

  • Demonstrate the handling of POSIX data and times using the Tidyverse library lubridate.

  • Demonstrate data preparation and combination of information from multiple tables using Tidyverse libraries dplyr and tidyr.

  • Possible extension of these analyses with mySQL and application of comparable functions for the much larger airlines dataset (difficult so far due to slow queries on KU-mySQL server).

Note in passing: You can also determine the coordinates of the three airports using the following function calls from the airports table in the R package nycflights13; latitude and longitudes differ slightly from the coordinates in airports_coord used above.

> nycflights13::airports |> 
+   filter(faa %in% c("JFK", "LGA", "EWR")) |> 
+   rename(airport = faa) |> 
+   select(airport, lat, lon)
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  airport   lat   lon
  <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 EWR      40.7 -74.2
2 JFK      40.6 -73.8
3 LGA      40.8 -73.9

  7. Data and especially URLs change frequently. It is therefore recommended that all information downloaded from the Internet, especially data and its description, is backed up locally and protected against overwriting. This backup is not yet guaranteed by the R code below. Often it makes sense to separate the import of data and basic processing from the actual data analysis, which is then based on locally stored files.↩︎

  9. Caution is advised with factor variables. Classic statistical R functions such as lm and anova, which use the formula interface, use the properties of the factor class in a positive sense, as suitable design matrices are constructed automatically. However, problems repeatedly occur, especially when analyzing extensive data records that are linked via keys (keys) – particularly when date and time information is included. For this reason, factor variables are nowadays only used in the modelling phase when analyzing large data sets; in data administration and exploratory data analysis, on the other hand, nominally scaled variables are often left in their original state as character strings (character), although this requires more storage space.↩︎

  10. Without loading the library, this is done by calling mosaic::tally or mosaic::favstats. Alternatively, the functions tally and favstats can be used directly after first loading mosaic using library(mosaic) or require(mosaic).↩︎

  11. Both the widely used dplyr library from the tidyverse and mosaic sometimes use identical names for different functions, e.g. the symbol tally. Therefore, the mosaic library is mostly not loaded, but used by combining the package name followed by two colons (::) as a prefix to the function name (e.g. by calling mosaic::tally).↩︎

  12. Modern Data Science with r, 2nd ed. (CRC-Press, 2021).↩︎

  13. A side note: The janitor library contains numerous auxiliary functions for data preparation and data exploration. This also includes functions that can be used to clean up variable names. Excel tables often use column names which, within the world of programming languages, are non-syntactic names (including the % sign) and can therefore only be used with difficulty (in R, for example, with backticks). The janitor function janitor::clean_names can be used to convert these variable names very quickly into syntactically valid names.↩︎
